paper_title: CONCOR: Benchmarking Contrastive Decoding for Visual Hallucination Mitigation Beyond Final-Output Performance

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Contrastive decoding (CD) mitigates object hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by contrasting token distributions under different conditions to adjust token scores. However, existing generative and discriminative benchmarks primarily measure final task scores, which can be confounded by candidate filtering, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases, making it difficult to isolate the effects of the underlying contrastive adjustments. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), a controlled benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates using the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM). CGM also enables analysis of directional consistency, composition, and reliability of contrastive corrections. Our evaluation reveals that existing CD methods exhibit distinct correction behaviors: some consistently favor ground-truth candidates, whereas others produce strong corrections but also introduce more errors. Crucially, these differences help explain their contrasting responses to increased contrast strength, which improves some methods while degrading others. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating the contrastive correction itself, rather than relying solely on final-output performance, and CONCOR provides a controlled and interpretable framework for understanding and improving CD methods for hallucination mitigation.

Introduction Recent advances in integrating vision encoders with large language models have endowed multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with broad, general-purpose capabilities in image and video description [23], visual question answering [3], multimodal dialogue [21], visual grounding [25], document understanding [7], and visual reasoning [27, 42]. Nevertheless, when visual evidence is weak or underutilized, these models often over-rely on linguistic priors and scene co-occurrence patterns, producing plausible yet visually unsupported objects, attributes, or relations [6, 11, 15, 22, 36]. This phenomenon, commonly known as visual hallucination [12, 24], undermines the trustworthiness of model outputs and limits deployment in high-reliability settings such as medical assistance and autonomous driving [1, 35, 46]. Researchers have explored training-time alignment [10, 29, 3941], post-hoc correction [16, 38, 45], and decodingtime intervention to mitigate visual hallucinations [8, 17, 1 31, 47]. Among these approaches, contrastive decoding (CD) has attracted considerable attention because it requires no additional training and operates directly at inference time [17, 30]. CD contrasts token distributions produced under different conditions and uses their differences to adjust next-token scores [13]. Mechanistically, CD provides effective correction only when the contrastive adjustment increases the relative preference for visually grounded candidate over candidate that lacks visual support. If this relative preference instead decreases, the contrastive intervention may reinforce the erroneous candidate. Existing methods typically assess CDs ability to mitigate hallucinations through scores on generative and discriminative tasks [4, 17, 33]. However, these scores are influenced by both decoding choices and task design. First, CD can benefit from shortcut to higher benchmark scores by adopting decoding strategy that filters out low-probability hallucinated tokens [37]. Second, generative evaluations apply CD throughout generation, where revisions to non-target content can alter the subsequent generation context and thereby affect later object decisions [32, 43, 44]. Third, accuracy in discriminative evaluations is sensitive to Yes/No response tendencies [19]. CD may therefore improve accuracy by increasing the rate of affirmative responses, allowing changes in response tendency to be counted as gains in hallucination mitigation. Together, these factors make it difficult to isolate the direct effect of contrastive intervention on object decisions from the reported final task scores. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), controlled benchmark for directly evaluating the competition between ground-truth and hallucinated candidates; see Appendix for details. CONCOR constructs candidate sets containing ground-truth objects and different types of hallucinated objects selected according to their co-occurrence relationships with the image content. All candidates are evaluated at the same decoding position and context, using logits extracted from the original and contrastive branches before candidate filtering. This design isolates the contrastive adjustment from downstream generation trajectories, candidate filtering, and response tendencies. Within CONCOR, we introduce the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM) to diagnose whether and how CD strengthens the relative advantage of ground-truth over hallucinated candidates. Beyond measuring the direction and magnitude of contrastive correction, CGM provides three complementary diagnostic properties including directional consistency, correction composition, and correction reliability. Our contributions are threefold: We identify how decoding constraints, generation trajectories, and response bias can confound existing generative and discriminative evaluations, obscuring the underlying contrastive correction produced by CD. We introduce CONCOR, controlled benchmark for directly evaluating competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates, together with CGM for measuring and diagnosing contrastive correction. We reveal substantial differences in the directional consistency, composition, and reliability of existing CD methods and how that these differences help explain why increasing contrast strength benefits some methods while degrading others, with the main patterns remaining robust across models and task settings. 2. Related Work Contrastive decoding. Existing contrastive decoding methods differ mainly in how they obtain the distributions used for comparison. VCD [17] perturbs the input image, ICD [33] introduces disturbance instructions , while SID [9] and AvisC [34] manipulate visual representations based on token relevance or attention. Other approaches construct contrast through confidence-aware logit calibration [13], image-unconditioned predictions [4], or intermediate-layer representations [2]. Despite these differences, these methods share the principle of contrasting alternative output distributions to adjust token predictions. Hallucination evaluation. Existing benchmarks evaluate multimodal hallucination through generative, discriminative, and combined settings. CHAIR measures object hallucination in image captioning by comparing generated object mentions with ground-truth image annotations [26]. It reports both the proportion of captions containing hallucinated objects and the proportion of hallucinated objects among all object mentions. POPE formulates object hallucination evaluation as binary existence questions and constructs negative samples using random, popular, and adversarial sampling strategies [19]. AMBER provides broader benchmark covering both generative and discriminative hallucination without relying on an external LLM evaluator. Its evaluation includes hallucinations involving objects, attributes, and relations [32]. Together, these benchmarks provide complementary measurements of object-level and response-level visual faithfulness and are widely used to assess hallucination mitigation methods in MLLMs [5]. 3. Limitations of Existing CD Evaluations Effective CD requires the contrastive branch to provide corrective signal favoring visually grounded over hallucinated object candidates. However, existing evaluations primarily assess CD using downstream generative and discriminative task scores, which do not necessarily isolate the effectiveness of this signal. Observation 1: Decoding constraints confound the evaluation of CDs corrective ability. Adaptive Plausibility Constraint (APC), commonly used in contrastive decoding methods [9, 17, 33], restricts the candidate tokens using the original branchs predicted probabilities. By filtering out low-probability candidates before final selection, APC can affect hallucination-related performance without necessarily strengthening the contrastive branchs corrective signal. Because CD is applied throughout autoregressive generation, it can alter not only object tokens but also non-target content, such as attributes and actions. These changes become part of the generation prefix and may subsequently influence object predictions. Observation 3: Discriminative evaluations can conflate response bias with improved hallucination mitigation. Effective CD should improve discrimination between objects that are present and absent in the image: predictions of present objects should increase, while false predictions of absent objects should decrease. However, prior work [37] demonstrates that discriminative scores can also be improved through an affirmative-answer shortcut using Prompt-Based Adjustment (PBA) and Output Layer Modification (OLM). CONCOR The preceding observations show that existing evaluation scores can be affected by decoding constraints, generation context, and response bias, making it difficult to isolate the corrective signal provided by the contrastive branch. Evaluating this signal therefore requires comparable object-decision conditions under which we can directly measure whether contrastive intervention increases the relative advantage of ground-truth over hallucinated candidates. We therefore introduce CONCOR (Contrastive Correction Evaluation), benchmark dataset that places ground-truth and hallucinated objects in the same multiple-choice candidate set, fixes the generation context and decoding position, and extracts raw logits from both branches without candidate filtering. Within CONCOR, we define the Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM) to measure the direction and magnitude of the resulting change in relative advantage (summarized in Figure 4). 5.1. Experiments We conduct experiments to evaluate existing CD methods through CONCOR and investigate how the diagnostic properties of CGM manifest in practice. Specifically, we organize our experiments around three research questions: RQ1. How effective are existing CD methods, and what contrastive correction patterns underlie their performance? RQ2. How does contrast strength affect these corrections and prediction performance? RQ3. Are the observed correction patterns consistent across models and task settings? 6.1. Setup We compare baseline decoding with VCD [17], ICD [33], SID [9], and AvisC [34] on CONCOR, covering the 7B and 13B variants of LLaVA-1.5 [21] and InstructBLIPVicuna [3], as well as single-answer and multiple-answer settings. brief introduction of the CD methods are provided in Appenix B. For each CD method, we extract raw logits from the original and contrastive branches at the first answer position before candidate filtering. We report mean CGM, the positive-CGM rate to measure the magnitude and directional consistency of the contrastive correction, respectively, together with image-level sampling accuracy to measure its effect on final predictions. 6.2. RQ1: How Effective Are Existing CD Methods? We first evaluate existing CD methods under the main setting of LLaVA-1.5-7B with single-answer questions. As shown in Table 2, Baseline decoding achieves an accuracy of 71.1%. The CD methods exhibit substantial differences in both prediction accuracy and their underlying contrastive corrections. VCD obtains mean CGM of 0.029 and positive-CGM rate of 41.6%, with accuracy decreasing to 69.2%. In contrast, ICD, SID, and AvisC achieve positive mean CGMs of 0.393, 1.279, and 3.254, respectively, and improve accuracy to 77.5%, 81.5%, and 83.1%. These results show that the performance differences among CD methods are associated with substantial differences in the contrastive corrections they produce. Directional consistency. CD methods differ substantially in the directional consistency of their contrastive adjustments. Table 3 shows that VCD has positive-CGM rate of only 41.6%, suggesting that its contrastive adjustments decrease rather than increase the ground-truth advantage on most samples. In contrast, ICD and AvisC achieve positive-CGM rates of 93.6% and 98.3%, respectively, indicating highly consistent correction toward the ground truth. SID falls between these methods, with positive-CGM rate of 74.7%: although its adjustments favor ground-truth candidates in most cases, they are less consistent than those of ICD and AvisC. These differences help distinguish methods that reliably apply corrections in the desired direction from those whose corrections are frequently misdirected. Correction composition. CD methods achieve positive correction through different candidate-level adjustment patterns. On successfully corrected samples, ICD makes small but relatively uniform adjustments to hallucinated candidates, decreasing the logits of the strongest and remaining hallucinations by 0.10 and 0.10, respectively. SID instead concentrates its adjustments on separating the ground truth from the strongest hallucination, raising the former by 2.05 and lowering the latter by 0.64, while the remaining hallucinations change by only +0.03. AvisC exhibits different pattern: it increases the logits of all three candidate groups by 17.44, 16.16, and 14.49. Because these increases are progressively smaller for the strongest and remaining hallucinations, AvisC increases the ground-truth margin over these groups by 1.28 and 2.95. These results show that positive contrastive correction can arise through different mechanisms, including direct suppression of hallucinated candidates or larger relative increase in ground-truth logits, even when hallucinated logits themselves increase. Across Models and Task Settings? The main differences among CD methods remain consistent across model architectures, parameter scales, and question formats. Table 2 shows that, when LLaVA-1.5-7B is replaced with InstructBLIP-Vicuna-7B, AvisC and SID achieve mean CGM values of 1.525 and 0.357 in the singleanswer setting, still exceeding VCDs 0.078 and ICDs 0.059. The same ordering is observed at larger model scale: on LLaVA-1.5-13B, AvisC and SID achieve mean CGM values of 4.683 and 4.151, compared with 0.178 for VCD and 0.120 for ICD. These results are aligned with the finding that feature-level methods provide stronger corrective signals across models. As shown in Figure 5, this consistency extends to multiple-answer tasks, where multiple ground-truth candidates jointly compete with hallucinated candidates. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, AvisC and SID achieve mean CGM values of 2.131 and 0.545, respectively, again exceeding ICDs 0.115 and VCDs 0.030. Across all eight settings comprising four model variants and two question formats in Table 2, AvisC consistently achieves higher mean CGM than SID, and both exceed the ICD and VCD. Additional analyses further confirm the robustness of these findings across different option-selection settings (Appendix C.6), levels of annotation missingness (Appendix D), and dataset construction (Appendix D.1). Conclusion We revisit the evaluation of contrastive decoding for mitigating object hallucinations in multimodal large language models. We show that existing generative and discriminative evaluations can be confounded by decoding constraints, changes in generation trajectories, and response biases. To address these limitations while complementing existing evaluations, we introduce CONCOR, benchmark that directly evaluates the competition between ground-truth and different types of hallucinated candidates, together with Contrastive Grounding Margin (CGM), which measures how contrastive decoding changes their relative logit margins. Beyond measuring the overall strength of contrastive correction, CGM provides diagnostics of its directional consistency, correction composition, and reliability. Applying this framework to existing CD methods reveals substantial differences in how they produce corrections. Looking forward, these diagnostics provide several directions for improving CD methods. For example, future work could develop contrastive branches that produce more consistently beneficial corrections, adapt contrast strength according to the direction and magnitude of the contrastive signal, or explicitly control how adjustments are distributed between ground-truth and hallucinated candidates. Together, CONCOR and CGM provide more controlled and interpretable framework for evaluating contrastive decoding and understanding how its underlying adjustments contribute to hallucination mitigation.

Robustness to Annotation Missingness COCO object annotations are not exhaustive. Consequently, an object that is present in an image but unannotated may be incorrectly treated as absent. This issue can affect not only the estimated object co-occurrence statistics but also the resulting hallucinated candidates. We therefore examine whether such annotation missingness alters our conclusions about contrastive correction produced by different methods. Experimental setup. We conduct the experiment on newly sampled set of 200 images and simulate incomplete annotations by artificially removing object-instance annotations. We consider two missingness mechanisms. Under uniform missingness, every eligible object instance has the same probability of being removed. Under small-objectprioritized missingness, smaller instances are more likely to be removed, approximating the greater likelihood that small objects are missed in image annotations. We consider missingness rates of = 10% and = 20%, where denotes the proportion of eligible object-instance annotations removed. Because different sets of removed annotations can affect benchmark construction differently even at the same missingness rate, we further examine this variation for = 10%. For each missingness mechanism, we generate 50 independent missingness realizations, each corresponding to different set of annotations removed at the same = 10% rate. We characterize the impact of each realization using two criteria. First, contaminated questions are questions in which an object removed from the annotations, but actually present in the image, is subsequently selected as hallucinated candidate. Second, changed questions are questions in which at least one structured hallucinated candidate differs from the = 0 setting. We rank the realizations first by the number of contaminated questions and then by the number of changed questions, and select the P10, P50, and P90 realizations as the mild, median, and severe conditions, respectively. These conditions have the same missingness rate but differ in how strongly the particular pattern of missing annotation affects benchmark construction. For every condition, we re-derive the image-level object sets, recompute the category co-occurrence probabilities, and reconstruct the three structured hallucinated candidates. The random hallucinated candidate is held fixed as control. Each question is evaluated with five cyclic answer-position permutations.
